prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Imagine two people, Alice and Bob, who have never met and who share nothing except a telephone line that anyone can tap. They want to agree on a secret number, perhaps to lock their later messages so that eavesdroppers cannot read them. At first this sounds impossible, because everything they say to each other is overheard, and a secret that has been spoken aloud is no longer a secret. The surprise of public-key cryptography is that it can be done, and the idea behind it is simpler than its reputation suggests.

The key insight is that some jobs are easy to do in one direction and extremely hard to undo. Mixing paint is the classic picture. Stirring two colours together takes a moment, but handing someone the finished mixture and asking them to separate it back into the original colours is hopeless. Now suppose Alice and Bob publicly agree on a common yellow paint. Alice secretly picks a private colour of her own, say red, and mixes it into the yellow. Bob secretly picks a private colour, say blue, and does the same. Each then sends the resulting mixture across the line for everyone to see. Alice now adds her private red to the mixture she received from Bob, and Bob adds his private blue to the mixture he received from Alice. Both end up with yellow, red and blue combined, so they hold exactly the same final colour. An eavesdropper saw only the yellow and the two half-mixed pots, and cannot unmix either pot to recover the private colour inside it. Adding a different colour to the pots would only produce a different final shade, not the one Alice and Bob share.

Paint is only a picture, so the real method replaces mixing with a kind of arithmetic that has the same one-way property. This arithmetic is a close cousin of reading a clock. On a clock with twelve hours, if it is ten o'clock and you wait five hours, you arrive at three o'clock, because the numbers wrap around after twelve. Mathematicians call this working modulo twelve, and you can do it with any size of clock. If we use a clock with 23 positions, then any number is replaced by its remainder after dividing by 23, so 25 becomes 2 and 46 becomes 0. This wrapping is the only unfamiliar idea you need, and everything else is ordinary multiplication and powers that you met at school.

Here is how Alice and Bob use it. They publicly agree on two numbers, and everyone is allowed to hear them. The first is the size of the clock, which we will take to be 23, and the second is a starting number, which we will take to be 5. Alice secretly chooses a private number, say 6, and Bob secretly chooses a private number, say 15. These private numbers are never spoken aloud, and they play the role of the secret paint colours.

Alice now multiplies 5 by itself 6 times, which gives 15,625, and then wraps this number around the 23-hour clock by taking the remainder after dividing by 23. The remainder is 8, and this is her public message, which she sends to Bob. Bob does the same with his private number, multiplying 5 by itself 15 times and wrapping around the clock, and his result is 19. He sends this to Alice. An eavesdropper therefore hears the numbers 23, 5, 8 and 19, and nothing else.

The next step is where the two sides arrive at the same secret. Alice takes the 19 she received from Bob and multiplies it by itself 6 times, which is her own private number, then wraps the result around the clock. She gets 2. Bob takes the 8 he received from Alice and multiplies it by itself 15 times, which is his private number, and wraps around the clock too. He also gets 2. The shared secret is 2, and neither of them ever had to say it aloud. The reason this works is a fact about powers that you can check yourself. Raising 5 to the power 6 and then raising that to the power 15 gives the same result as raising 5 to the power 15 and then to the power 6, because both equal 5 raised to the power 90. The order in which the two private numbers are applied does not matter, so both people reach the same answer by different routes.

You may wonder why an eavesdropper cannot simply work backwards. The eavesdropper knows that 5 raised to some power gives 8 on the 23-hour clock, and could try every power in turn until one matches. With a clock of only 23 positions, this takes seconds, and the secret of 2 would be found at once. The protection comes from making the clock enormous. In real use the clock has hundreds of digits, and the private numbers are similarly huge. Computing the forward direction is still quick, because clever shortcuts let a computer handle even gigantic powers in a fraction of a second. Working backwards, however, offers no known shortcut, and trying every possibility would take longer than the age of the universe on every computer in existence. The method is secure not because the eavesdropper is missing any information, but because using that information to recover the secret is far too much work.

This method is often described as public-key cryptography because each person ends up with a pair of numbers. The private number stays hidden, and the public number, like Alice's 8 or Bob's 19, can be shouted to the world. A close relative of the idea works for sending secret messages directly. Someone publishes a public key, which works like an open padlock that anybody can snap shut. Only the owner holds the private key that can open it. Anyone may lock a message with the padlock, but only the owner can read it, and so strangers can write to each other privately without ever having met.

Once the two people share a secret number, they use it as the key for a much faster, simpler scrambling method that works in both directions, and this scrambled conversation protects the rest of their exchange. This is what happens every time your browser shows a padlock beside a web address. Your computer and the website agree on a shared secret in a fraction of a second, over a connection that countless strangers could in principle be watching, and then use it to protect your passwords and card details.

One honest caveat remains. The method proves that two parties share a secret, but it does not prove who the other party is, so an impostor who sits in the middle of the line could trick both sides. Real systems therefore add certificates, which are digital proofs of identity, on top of the arithmetic described here. The core idea stands, though. By letting each person keep one ingredient private and publish a blended version, two strangers can build a shared secret in plain sight, and the only thing standing between an eavesdropper and that secret is a calculation that is easy in one direction and impossibly slow in the other.
